chapter.title: Two more houses catch: Russia and America join

cards.body: In six months of 1941, Hitler picked fights with the two biggest powers on earth, and the second one he didn't even have to. On our street, that's the fire spreading on purpose into the two largest houses, the ones with the deepest wells and the most hoses. **Every hose they owned would now point back at him.**
cards.simpler: In six months of 1941, Hitler started fights with the two biggest powers in the world. He didn't even have to start the second one. Picture our street: it's like the fire spreading on purpose into the two largest houses, the ones with the deepest wells and the most hoses. **Every hose they owned would now point back at him.**

cards.prompt: 22 June 1941. About 3 million German soldiers cross into the Soviet Union, along a front running from the Baltic Sea to the Black Sea. How long did Hitler expect this to take?

options.text: Years: he knew it would be a long, grinding war
A few months: finished before the winter snow
No plan at all: he only invaded because Stalin attacked first

whyNot.a: That's what the war turned into, not what he planned: German troops were badly short of winter clothing when the snow came.
whyNot.c: That gets the roles backwards: Germany attacked first and broke its own 1939 pact with Stalin.

cards.reteach: Hitler had just watched France fall in six weeks. He expected the Soviet Union to fall the same way, fast. He was planning for a short fire, not a long one.

cards.title: Why Russia
cards.body:
Hitler had said it for years: Germany's future lay in *living space*, his phrase for farmland taken from the peoples of the east. The 1939 pact with Stalin was a pause, not a friendship. On 22 June 1941 he tore it up.

He planned it as a *war of extermination*, meaning a war to wipe people out, not just beat their army. Behind the tanks came killing squads that shot Jewish families at the edge of their own towns.

You'd think Russia's size would scare him off. It didn't. He was betting on **a quick knockout**, with the Soviet state collapsing before the snow.
cards.simpler: For years Hitler said Germany's future lay in 'living space'. By that he meant farmland taken from the peoples of the east. His 1939 deal with Stalin was a pause, not a friendship. On 22 June 1941 he broke it. He planned to wipe people out, not just beat an army. Killing squads followed the tanks and shot Jewish families outside their own towns. Russia's size didn't scare him. He was betting on **a quick knockout**, with the Soviet state collapsing before the snow.

cards.title: Sunday morning in Hawaii
cards.body: Sunday morning, 7 December 1941, Pearl Harbor, Hawaii. Planes from six Japanese aircraft carriers hit the American Pacific Fleet while it sat at anchor, and more than 2,400 Americans died. Japan's motive was oil: America had cut off Japan's oil that summer to push it into ending its war in China, and the nearest oil fields were to the south, in the Dutch East Indies, today's Indonesia. The plan was **to knock America flat long enough to grab them**. One problem: America's aircraft carriers were away from Pearl Harbor that morning, so none of them was in the harbour.
cards.simpler: Sunday morning, 7 December 1941. Planes from six Japanese aircraft carriers hit the American Pacific Fleet while it sat at anchor in Pearl Harbor, Hawaii. More than 2,400 Americans died. Japan wanted oil. That summer America had cut off Japan's oil to push it to end its war in China. The nearest oil fields were to the south, in today's Indonesia. The plan was **to knock America flat long enough to grab them**. But America's aircraft carriers were away from Pearl Harbor that morning.

cards.prompt: Tokyo, autumn 1941. Japan's leaders are weighing an attack on the American fleet. Which plan matches what they were actually betting on?

options.text: Land troops in California and march on Washington
Wreck the fleet, grab the oil to the south, and hope a stunned America makes a deal instead of fighting a long war
Stay clear of American territory so America never joins in

whyNot.a: That's a film plot, not the real plan: Japan wanted the oil to the south, not American land.
whyNot.c: That's the opposite of what they chose: Hawaii was American, and hitting it was the point.

cards.reteach: Japan's bet had the same shape as Hitler's in June: one heavy blow and a fast grab, done before the bigger side could fight back. A long war was the one thing they could not afford.

cards.title: The choice nobody forced
cards.body:
On 11 December 1941, four days after Pearl Harbor, Hitler declared war on the United States. No treaty made him do it. Germany's pact with Japan only promised help if someone attacked Japan, and Japan had done the attacking.

His reasoning: America was already shipping weapons to Britain and guarding supply ships in the Atlantic, so it was half in already. And Japan would keep it busy in the Pacific.

Now look down the street. Britain, the Soviet Union and America had far more people, oil and factories than Germany, Italy and Japan put together. **Germany needed a short war. Now it had a long one.**
cards.simpler: On 11 December 1941, four days after Pearl Harbor, Hitler declared war on America. No treaty forced him. His deal with Japan only covered Japan being attacked, and Japan had attacked first. He figured America was half in, since it was sending Britain weapons and guarding Atlantic ships. Japan would keep it busy. But Britain, the Soviet Union and America had far more people, oil and factories than Germany, Italy and Japan. **Germany needed a short war. Now it had a long one.**

cards.body: Sam reads that by December 1941 Germany was fighting Britain, Russia and America, and decides the war was basically over. Then Sam can't work out why it went on for more than three years. **Winning on paper is not winning on the battlefield**: German troops were still deep inside Russia, and Japan kept winning for six more months. Factories take years to turn into tanks.
cards.simpler: Sam reads that by December 1941 Germany was fighting Britain, Russia and America. Sam decides the war was as good as over. Then Sam can't work out why it went on for more than three years. **Winning on paper is not winning on the battlefield.** German troops were still deep inside Russia, and Japan kept winning for six more months. Factories take years to turn into tanks.

cards.prompt: A friend asks what really changed in 1941. Which answer gets it right?

options.text: America declared war on Germany after Pearl Harbor, pulling Hitler in against his will
Germany and Japan each hit a giant hoping for a fast knockout. It didn't come, so they faced a long war against far bigger enemies
The Allies won the battles that decided the war

whyNot.a: That's the order flipped: Hitler declared war on America himself, four days after Pearl Harbor.
whyNot.c: That mixes up winning on paper with winning on the battlefield: in December 1941, German troops were still deep in Russia and Japan was still winning.

cards.reteach: Think of 1941 as two gambles on speed. A fast win would have kept the giants down. Neither win came, and a slow war meant fighting countries with far more of everything.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body: In 1941 Hitler invaded the Soviet Union and Japan bombed Pearl Harbor, each **betting on a knockout before the giant could fight back**. Neither giant went down, and once Hitler chose to declare war on America too, Germany was stuck in a long war against enemies with far more people, oil and factories.
cards.simpler: In 1941 Hitler invaded the Soviet Union and Japan bombed Pearl Harbor. Both were **betting on a knockout before the giant could fight back**. Neither giant fell. Then Hitler chose to declare war on America too. That left Germany stuck in a long war against enemies with far more people, oil and factories.

cards.body: Open your map app and zoom out until Hawaii and Moscow fit on one screen: that is how far apart the two 1941 bets were. Tomorrow: the three battles where the fire finally stopped spreading.
cards.simpler: Open your map app. Zoom out until you can see Hawaii and Moscow on one screen. That is how far apart **the two 1941 bets** were. Tomorrow: the three battles where the fire finally stopped spreading.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now explain why 1941 turned a European war into a world war, and why it left Germany outmatched on paper.

dubious_claims: 'America's aircraft carriers were out at sea that morning' is imprecise: Enterprise and Lexington were at sea, but Saratoga was docked at San Diego. Say 'away from Pearl Harbor' instead.
'Most German soldiers had no winter coats when the snow came' is a widely repeated simplification. Winter clothing was badly short, but 'most' is hard to source.
'About 3 million German soldiers' is a fair round figure for the Germans alone. The total Axis invasion force was about 3.8 million, so keep 'German' explicit.
repairedFrom.why: The try card ends the chapter flat after the 'Tomorrow' hook. It also asks for four fingers on the phone the reader is holding, and it buries the open loop one card early.
repairedFrom.fix: Rewrite the try card as: 'Open your map app and zoom out until Hawaii and Moscow fit on one screen: that is how far apart the two 1941 bets were. Tomorrow: the three battles where the fire finally stopped spreading.' Then cut the 'Tomorrow' line from the 'In one breath' card.
